profiles.meeting_scenario: A 45-minute brainstorming meeting between an academic research lead and an executive education design lead at a business school–industry center. They are preparing a proposal for a fall consortium session and accompanying short briefing note on the seed topic: whether dynamic capabilities in established firms come mainly from routinized organizational processes or from entrepreneurial action by a few senior executives. The context is that several member firms in the center—spanning industrial equipment, SaaS, and healthcare services—have asked for a session that is intellectually rigorous but also usable for senior managers. The agenda is to generate and screen 3-4 possible session concepts, examples, and framing devices for the proposal. The expected outcome is a shortlist of promising concepts, a rough audience framing, and agreement on what kind of illustrative material to pull together next.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Faculty Director, Strategy and Transformation Lab
members.expertise: Dynamic capabilities, qualitative case research, corporate transformation, strategy theory
members.background: Elena is a strategy professor who previously worked in restructuring advisory before moving into academia; she often turns executive phenomena into teaching cases and research briefs for senior leadership audiences.
members.private_state: She wants the proposal to be intellectually distinctive enough to become a publishable managerial article later, and she is wary of the session collapsing into generic leadership advice.
hidden_assumptions: If a capability is said to be 'routinized,' there should be some identifiable decision architecture, governance mechanism, or codified pattern that outlives the focal executive.
A useful session on entrepreneurial management should stay focused on the true top-management layer because the core theoretical claim concerns asset orchestration at the apex of the firm.
A strong illustrative case is one that reveals mechanism through a sharp before-and-after contrast, even if it comes from only one or two firms.
When people mention the 'Apple example' in this debate, they usually mean the Steve Jobs absence/return episode as evidence that individual executives can matter beyond routines.

members.name: Marcus Reed
members.role: Program Design Lead, Executive Learning Partnerships
members.expertise: Executive workshop design, leadership development, applied organizational psychology, consortium programming
members.background: Marcus designs cross-industry sessions for corporate member firms and previously led leadership programs inside a large multinational, where he translated academic ideas into practical tools for divisional leaders.
members.private_state: He wants the proposal to land with member firms as immediately applicable and scalable, and he is concerned that a theory-heavy concept centered on rare CEOs will feel irrelevant to the managers who actually attend.
hidden_assumptions: If something is 'routinized' in a useful managerial sense, it can be spread through talent systems, shared language, and recurring leadership forums even without heavy codification.
The relevant 'leadership layer' for a consortium session includes business-unit leaders and transformation office heads, not just the CEO and C-suite.
An idea becomes credible for executive audiences when it is supported by several recognizable company examples and yields reusable managerial prompts.
When people invoke the 'Apple case' here, they usually mean Apple University and similar efforts to propagate top-management judgment into the organization.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether firms can 'routinize' sensing, seizing, and transformation without killing entrepreneurship.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means formalized or at least stable organizational mechanisms—decision rules, governance forums, selection routines, and codified patterns—that can be analytically identified as organizational rather than personal.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means practical diffusion of judgment through leader development, repeated conversations, mentoring, and shared heuristics, even if the process stays largely tacit and socially carried.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In strategy-and-leadership settings, both meanings are commonly bundled together under the same verb, and both speakers are positively disposed toward partial routinization rather than full automation, so the wording feels aligned.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the session should target the 'leadership layer' that shapes dynamic capabilities.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the discussion centers on the CEO, a few C-suite executives, and possibly board-level influence because the underlying claim is about top-management asset orchestration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the discussion includes division presidents, general managers, innovation heads, and transformation office leaders because those are the realistic participants and change carriers in member firms.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'leadership layer' is naturally vague and sounds appropriately strategic; each person hears a sensible audience that fits their own context, so neither sees a reason to unpack the boundary.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes an example 'credible' enough for the proposal
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need a few 'credible examples' to anchor the concept note.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks credibility comes from examples with clear causal contrast and mechanism, such as a founder-return episode or a transformation under a specific executive where one can trace sensing, seizing, and transforming decisions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks credibility comes from having several familiar firms across industries so executives see the pattern as broadly usable, even if each example is lighter and more illustrative than deeply causal.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using 'credible' as praise for evidence quality, but one is applying a research-style threshold while the other is applying a practitioner-recognition threshold; in a brainstorming meeting, this difference sounds like complementary emphasis rather than divergence.

misalignment_points.topic: Which Apple episode is serving as the anchor example
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the Apple example' as a way to show the relationship between individual executives and routines.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of Steve Jobs's removal and return, using Apple's performance swings as a quasi-natural experiment showing dependence on entrepreneurial managerial action.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of Apple University and the internal teaching of key decisions as an example of embedding founder-like judgment into organizational practice.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Apple is so canonical in this literature that naming the company alone creates strong apparent common ground, and both episodes genuinely support the broader topic, so the reference mismatch passes unnoticed.

turns.inner_thought: I need to frame this tightly enough that it could later become a serious managerial article, not another vague leadership session. The intellectual core is the tension in dynamic capabilities between organizational processes and the entrepreneurial action of a few apex executives. If we drift into generic advice for broad manager populations, the theoretical contribution disappears.
turns.utterance: I think the proposal writes itself if we center the basic tension clearly: in established firms, do dynamic capabilities come mainly from routines, or do they depend on entrepreneurial action by senior executives? If we can shape that into a session that feels rigorous but still useful to the consortium, we’ll have something strong.

turns.inner_thought: Good opening. I need to keep this from sounding like a debate about rare superstar CEOs, because our member firms will send business-unit and transformation leaders, not just people at the very top. If we position it for the leadership layer that shapes dynamic capabilities, it will feel relevant to who actually shows up.
turns.utterance: Yes, and the sweet spot for me is a discussion for the leadership layer that shapes dynamic capabilities—something that helps firms see when transformation depends more on people and when it depends more on process, without drifting into hero-CEO mythology.

turns.inner_thought: A first concept could ask whether firms can actually routinize sensing and seizing once a standout chief executive has demonstrated the pattern. The Apple example is the obvious anchor because the Jobs absence-and-return arc gives a sharp before-and-after contrast and lets us ask whether the capability resided in the organization or in the executive.
turns.utterance: One possible concept is to build the session around whether firms can routinize sensing and seizing after a standout executive has shown the way. The Apple example is an obvious anchor for that conversation.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—Apple is useful because people immediately recognize the effort to carry judgment beyond one person. If we talk about routinizing in a practical sense, we can get leaders thinking about how judgment gets propagated through the organization so others can use it. That makes the topic actionable for the participant group I have in mind.
turns.utterance: I like the Apple example precisely because it lets us show how judgment can be propagated and routinized enough for other leaders to use it. That could make the whole session feel much more practical for the audience.

turns.inner_thought: We need sharper evidentiary anchors than just a broad Apple mention. I want one or two contrast cases where a small top-management group clearly made or failed to make the difference, so the note has mechanism rather than a pile of anecdotes. Credible examples should reveal causality, not just familiarity.
turns.utterance: Then maybe we pair Apple with one or two sharp contrast cases, so the note has a few credible examples that show when dynamic capabilities really rest on a small top-management group.

turns.inner_thought: I should broaden this out. For executives in the room, credibility comes from seeing several recognizable companies across sectors, not just one deep dive. And I need material that can convert into prompts the leadership layer can actually discuss together, otherwise the note will feel too academic.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I’d just say credibility will improve if we can point to several recognizable firms from different sectors and translate each one into prompts the leadership layer can discuss in the room.

turns.inner_thought: A second concept should move beyond the founder-versus-routine framing and get to asset orchestration, which is the real strategic heart of dynamic capabilities. The important decisions are enterprise-level calls about alliances, acquisitions, and redeployment made before there is any established structure to guide them—again, this is top-management work.
turns.utterance: A second concept could focus more explicitly on asset orchestration—how executives decide when alliances, acquisitions, or internal redeployment should happen before any routine exists to guide them.

turns.inner_thought: That’s useful if I can turn it into something scalable. I’m hearing an opening to ask how entrepreneurial calls become routinized through reviews, talent discussions, and recurring strategic conversations, because that’s the kind of infrastructure organizations can actually build and leaders below the C-suite can influence.
turns.utterance: Yes, and we could build on that by asking how far those entrepreneurial calls can be routinized into reviews, talent forums, and recurring strategic conversations so the capability actually scales.

turns.inner_thought: I should narrow us before this expands too far. The proposal needs to stay centered on the leadership layer closest to enterprise-wide reconfiguration, otherwise we lose the theoretical edge. And for the concept note, I want a short list of maybe two or three examples with enough analytical bite to show mechanism cleanly.
turns.utterance: Agreed. For the proposal, I’d keep it centered on the leadership layer closest to major reconfiguration and draft a short list of two or three credible examples for the concept note.

turns.inner_thought: This is landing well. I can summarize it in a way that sounds coherent to both of us and useful to member firms: a session on how organizations move from founder- or executive-led insight toward routinized transformation capacity, anchored by Apple plus a few other familiar cases. Later I can shape the audience framing and exercises around the broader leadership group I expect in the room.
turns.utterance: So the through-line is a session on how firms move from founder- or executive-led insight toward routinized transformation capacity, with Apple and a few other examples to make it concrete. If we write it that way, I think we can satisfy both the rigor and usability brief.
